problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.   Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.

activity_context.topic_title: Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Euclidean Spaces (Orthogonal Bases)

examples.problem:
Consider the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf v,\mathbf w\}$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14068823/assets/665de193fe6fda3cfc5b5ec38f61f2b69ccb0e5d72514d6622b0815c5c3f474b.png)
Find the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\}$ is orthogonal.
examples.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} 
= \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{x} + \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{w}}\mathbf{x}.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}\}$ and $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{w}\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{\sqrt{10}\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{\sqrt{10}\cdot 0+3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}w=(-1)[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ So, computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}\,x}{‖x‖\,‖{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}\cdot 0+3\cdot 3+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{(\sqrt{10})}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{10}{\sqrt{20}\,\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{10}{10\,\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta = \arccos\left( \dfrac{{\sqrt2}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

feedback.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is orthogonal.
feedback.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}},$ $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}},$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{3}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{3\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 4+(-9)\cdot 1+3\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=(-1)[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}], \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{3\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 0+(-9)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{3\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-9)\cdot 0+3\cdot 4}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}}{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-0)^{2}+(-3-(-5))^{2}+(-9-(-2))^{2}+(3-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{63} \\  & =3\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$
